title: Benares inscription of Pantha
html:
BENARES INSCRIPTION OF PANTHA.

BY P. DAYA RAM SAHNI.

I edit this inscription from two rubbings kindly supplied to me, one by Dr. J. Ph. Vogel, Superintendent, Archæological Survey, Northern Circle, and the other by Mr. G. D. Ganguli, Curator, Provincial Museum, Lucknow. A transcript of it has been published before in 1886 by Prof. Hultzsch in the Zeitschrift der Deutschen Morgenländischen Gesellschaft, Vol. XL. p. 55.

The slab on which the inscription is engraved is said to have been discovered in the vicinity of the modern city of Benares, and is one of the twenty-four objects which were presented. at the instance of Mr. J. H. Marshall, to the Lucknow Museum by the Principal of Queen's College, Benares, in December 1903.10 In discussing these sculptures, Dr. Vogel also noticed this stone, but failed to ascertain its precise find-spot.11

Judging from the rubbings, the slab which bears the extant portion of the inscription measures 26" by 15" (66 cm. by 38 cm.). The stone-mason has done his work with great care and neatness, and the letters are deeply cut.

The inscription consists of eight lines, but it is far from complete. About one-fifth of the entire slab is broken away along the proper left edge, and consequently lines 1-7 have each lost a number of syllables, which varies from nine to fourteen. The first three syllables of the first line and the first akshara of the second line have also disappeared owing to a small piece of stone having chipped off from the upper right corner. The record is further damaged by the surface having more or less peeled off in the marginal portions.

The characters of the inscription very closely resemble those of an inscription from Jhálrápátan12 and are of the ornamental type current in Northern India about the beginning of the eighth century A.D. Attention must, however, be drawn to the letters bh and y.13 The former of these always, and the latter in several cases, exhibit forms which come very close to those of the Maukhari alphabet of the sixth century A.D. The language is correct Sanskrit and metrical throughout. As regards orthography, there are three different points which deserve notice: (1) the doubling of the letters m, t, p and v in conjunction with a preceding or following r, in -maraṇayór=mmôksha-, l. 1; yattra, l. 2; attra and -múrttih, l. 4; sarppat-sarppa- and -ruchir=vvilóla-, l. 6; (2) the substitution of a single consonant for a double one in -tatva-, l. 3; -vrityá, l. 4; ujvalam, l. 7; and (3) the use of v for b in vrahmahá, l. 2, and sandhivandha-, l. 7.

The inscription is not dated, and its object is to record the erection of a shrine of Bhavânî at Benares. There are altogether five verses, the first three in the Sragdharâ and the last two in the Śárdálavikriđita metre. The first stanza is devoted to the praise of the city of Vârâṇasî. The purport of the second verse is not quite certain; it seems to speak of a particular quarter of the holy city, which was often visited even by the moon when practising her penance. The third verse contains an eulogy of the builder of the shrine, named Pantha, and the last two speak of the consecration of the Bhavânî image (?) and the construction of the shrine, respectively.

TEXT.

  1. 1 [Ôm svasti ||*] [Khyâ]tâ Vârâṇas=íyam tribhuvana-bhavan-âbhôga-chaur=íti dúrât=sèvantê yâm viraktâ janana-maraṇayór=mmôksha-sakt-aika-[chi]ttâh. [||] sô — — — —
  2. 2 [ta] sagaṇô yattra dêvô vimuktaḥ yâm drishtvâ vra(bra)hmah=ápi chyuta-kali-kalushô jáyatê śuddha-bhávaḥ || [1*] Asyâm=uttuṅga-śriṅga-sphuṭa-śa[śi]-kiraṇa-[śvêta-bhâsâ sanâtham ramy-âyâma*]-
  3. 3 pratôlî-vividha-jatapada-strî-vilâs-âbhirâmam | vidyâ-vêdârtha-tatva(ttva)-vrata-japa-niyama-vyagra-chandr-âbhijushtam śrîmat=sthânam [prî]thivyâ — — — —
  4. 4 Attr=âbhût=Pantha-nâmâ śisur=api vinaya-vyâpatô bhadra-múrttih tyâgî dhîraḥ kritajñaḥ parilaghu-vibhavô=py=âtma-15vrity(tty)=âbhitu[shṭaḥ15 | Gaṅgâ-srôtaś-śuchi-śrî*]-

5 Himagiri-śikhar-ārôha-khêdád=ritê=mbhah bhaktô bhaktyâ Śivô mê parishad=api gunais=tôshitâ yêna nityaân || [3*] Tên=ânêka-vidhâna-dikshaṇa-[śataih sainsthâpit=lârtha-vyayaih*]

6 chaṇđi chaṇda-narôttamânga-rachita-vyâlambi-mâl-ôtkaṭâ | sarppat-sarppa-vivêshtitânga-paraśu-vyâviddha-śushk-âmishâ lîlâ-nritta-ruchir=vvilô[la-18nayanâ mûrtir=19 Bhavânyâh śubhâ || 4*]

7 [Sainsthâ]py=âpi na tasya [tushti]r-a[bha]vad=yâvad=Bhavâni-grîham suślishti-âmala-sandhiva(ba)ndha-ghaṭitaân ghanṭâ-ninâd-ójva(jjva)laân | ramyatân drishṭi-haraâm śilâ

8 [prârûḍha]-dhvaja-châmaraâm su[kri]tinâ śrêyô-rthinâ kâritaân || [5*]

TRANSLATION.

[Ôm. Hail!] (Verse 1.) Famous is this Vârâṇasî which, having usurped the extent20 of the abode of the three worlds, is worshipped from afar by passionless people, with their mind solely fixed on liberation from birth and death; at which place was emancipated the god21 . . . with his attendants; and at the sight of which even the murderer of a Brâhmaṇâ, freed of the stain of sin, becomes pure of heart.

(V. 2.) In this (city there was) a place, renowned on earth; [bathed in the white light] of the bright rays of the moon (as they fell on its) lofty turrets; charming with the gracefulness of the wives of the various inhabitants of the [beautiful and extensive]22 streets; a favourite resort of the moon23 engaged in study, interpretation of the Vôdas, (search after) truth, (observance of) vows, muttering of prayers and austerities . . .

(V. 3.) Here lived (a man) named Pantha, who even as a child was well-behaved,24 handsome, generous, wise, grateful. (and) contented with his earnings in spite of his limited means; (who used to think thus to himself): 'The god (ambhah)25 Śiva is worshipped by my devotion without the toil of ascending the peaks of the Himâlaya, [purified by the waves of the Ganges];' and who constantly gladdened the assembly (of the wise) by (his) virtues.

(V. 4.) By him [was erected at a considerable cost (and) [with hundreds of] different consecrations [a beautiful image of Bhavâni], fierce-looking, awe-inspiring owing to a garland formed of gruesome human heads hanging (from her neck); with limbs encircled by crawling snakes, and with dry flesh pierced on an axe; delighting in a sportive dance, (and) with rolling [eyes].

(V. 5.) Not satisfied with the erection (of this image only), the pious man, desirous of bliss, caused to be built a shrine of Bhavānī, which was joined with a very adhesive and bright cement, resplendent with the sound of bells, lovely, attractive, . . . . . (and decorated) with lofty flags and yak-tails.

Footnotes

1(p. 59, n. 1) This word looks almost like narakô.

2(p. 59, n. 2) Read bhâmis=.

3(p. 59, n. 3) Literally, 'the village.'

4(p. 59, n. 4) This looks like a Dravidian word, which however cannot be traced in the dictionaries. The plates of Vijaya-Nandivarman (l. 4) seem to read, instead of it, Munuđa; but the apparent nu in the middle of this word may be in reality an obliterated nu.

5(p. 59, n. 5) The genitive bhagavato refers to Chittarathasâmi, the first member of the following compound. This is of course a grammatical blunder of the officer who drafted the inscription.

6(p. 59, n. 6) The pronoun 'this' evidently had been uttered by the king in the presence of the donee, just as otêshâm in the plates of Vijaya-Nandivarman, l. 5.

7(p. 59, n. 7) Prof. Kielhorn suggests to me that this doubtful word may be meant for Babhru.

8(p. 59, n. 8) On ardhika or ardhastrin see the Mitâksharâ on Yâjñavalkya, I. 166. The Prâkrit form addhika occurs in Ep. Ind. Vol. I. p. 6, text line 39.

9(p. 59, n. 9) The Sanskrit original of duvagga seems to be dvârga, which may be taken in the sense of dvâhetha.

10↩(p. 60, n. 1) Annual Report of the Lucknow Provincial Museum for 1903-4, p. 2.

11↩(p. 60, n. 2) Archæological Survey Report for 1903-4, p. 212.

12↩(p. 60, n. 3) Ind. Ant. Vol. V. p. 180 and Plate.

13↩(p. 60, n. 4) E.g. in yattra, jáyatê, l. 2; vinaya, l. 4; and yêna, l. 5.

14(p. 60, n. 5) [In my own transcript this word was misread as =árya-.—E. H.]

15↩(p. 60, n. 6) This restoration is based on the preceding abhitu16(p. 60, n. o) and âtma-vrittyâ.

17(p. 61, n. 1) Compare the expression sainsthâpya in l. 7.

18↩(p. 61, n. 2) This syllable is required to complete the word vilôla.

19↩(p. 61, n. 3) The restoration of mûrtir=, etc., is purely conjectural; but that it is probably correct, may be concluded from the fact that the epithets chaṇđi, etc., clearly refer to an image of Bhavâni. Moreover, since the very next verse records the foundation of a Bhavâni shrine, it seems almost necessary to assume that an image of the same goddess should have been placed in this shrine.

20↩(p. 61, n. 4) Literally, 'the thief of the extent,' etc.

21↩(p. 61, n. 5) This passage presumably alludes to Śiva's residence at Benares in the Trêtáyuga. See Rajendralal Mitra's Antiquities of Orissa, Vol. II. p. 63.

22↩(p. 61, n. 6) Literally, 'whose extent was charming.'

23↩(p. 61, n. 7) -bhakt-d̂bhijushtaâm would be a better reading.—[Or chandra may be meant for nara-chandra, 'an excellent man.'—E. H.]

24↩(p. 61, n. 8) I do not find the word vyápaṭa in any Sanskrit Dictionary. Vyápritô would be a more appropriate reading.

25↩(p. 61, n. 9) [But ambhah does not mean 'a god.' I would rather conjecture at the end of line 4 Gaṅgâyá dáhamânô and translate: 'devoutly (bhaktah) [entering] the water (ambhah) [of the Gaṅgâ].' In the following I prefer to join Śivômé and to translate: 'who daily pleased Śiva and Umâ by (his) devotion (and their) attendants by (his) virtues.'—E. H.]
